html:
The Chola bronzes are images of Hindu gods cast in the Tamil country under the Chola Empire, mainly between about 950 and 1250. They are among the finest metal sculptures ever made.

They were made to move. The stone image in a temple's inner room stays fixed, so a bronze double was carried out through the streets on festival days, dressed in silk and flowers. Holes in the base took the carrying poles.

Each is cast by the lost-wax method. The sculptor models the figure in wax, coats it in clay, melts the wax out and pours metal in. The mould is broken to free the image, so every piece is one of a kind.

The best known form is Nataraja, Shiva as lord of the dance. He dances inside a ring of fire with one leg lifted, a drum in one hand and a flame in another, and crushes a dwarf who stands for ignorance. The form was fixed in the 10th century, when Queen Sembiyan Mahadevi paid for many temples and images.

The sculptor Rodin wrote in praise of a Nataraja in 1913. A two-metre one, a gift from India, stands at the CERN physics laboratory near Geneva. Craftsmen at Swamimalai still cast the same way.
sum: The Chola bronzes are images of Hindu gods cast in the Tamil country under the Chola Empire, mainly between about 950 and 1250. They are among the finest metal sculptures ever made.
